38b8b0eb02bd2b8a.subject: Should I Get a Gun?
38b8b0eb02bd2b8a.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/cp/209673247

“You’re getting killed in the comments!” It’s not a text any writer wants to receive, but I wasn’t surprised. After all, I’d just written a piece [ https://substack.com/redirect/45bed606-f917-4d21-858b-6fce22f645ad?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] that was gently critical of America, and Free Press readers are a patriotic bunch; of course you leapt to your country’s defense.
For context: I’m British, I’d just been in an active-shooter situation in Washington, D.C., and I was reflecting on the Second Amendment. “Is it worth it letting civilians have guns? Does it really make this country more free?” I wrote. “Can you explain it to me? I want to know.”
I meant what I said. I genuinely wanted to hear from someone who believes what half the American population believe [ https://substack.com/redirect/0a47b46b-f6ae-4ca7-b5bf-42da522595f5?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]s: That it’s important to protect a citizen’s right to bear arms. The whole point—and the privilege—of being a journalist is getting into the hearts and minds of people who think differently.
Which brings me back to that text I got—the one about being killed in the comments.
It was from my friend and colleague Larissa Phillips, who I’ve edited since she joined The Free Press two years ago—and who happened to be perfectly placed to answer my appeal: “Help me understand.” Because once upon a time, Larissa herself was vehemently anti-gun—and now, she’s planning to get one.
A thread that runs through a lot of Larissa’s writing [ https://substack.com/redirect/01860965-f0da-40a9-b58d-a117653166fb?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] here at The Free Press is how moving from bright-blue Brooklyn to a red area of upstate New York changed her perspective—on Republicans [ https://substack.com/redirect/f6e4d83e-b81e-47f0-a1c8-4326ea9e7831?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], on marriage [ https://substack.com/redirect/2afa964f-66a1-435c-85fe-352d893368f9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], on America itself [ https://substack.com/redirect/280fa4fc-27dd-4f17-a799-f026b2e76113?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. In today’s essay, she writes that when she left New York City, she wouldn’t even let her kids have a water gun, but moving to a part of the country where firearms are a part of daily life, she slowly came to question her assumptions about the Americans who owned and used them.
This is the story of how she fired a bullet for the first time.  —Freya Sanders
I jammed my palm right up against the grip, wrapped fingers around my firing hand, extended both arms, and squinted at the target through my glasses. With all systems in place, there was nothing left to do but pull the trigger. Bam! At a velocity of about 800 mph, the bullet shot down the barrel of the gun in my hand and seemed to instantaneously punch through the target. I checked my handiwork. A tiny hole had appeared just a couple inches south of the white circle in the middle. Not bad for my first time ever firing a pistol. I looked at my instructor. “Can I go again?”
Until very recently, I could not have imagined taking lessons on how to shoot a handgun. I have spent most of my life extremely opposed to every single type of firearm. Guns are involved in most murders; they escalate volatile situations, land hotheaded young men in prison, and kill innocent people. I grew up the child of two anti-war idealists who deplored violence, and as a suburban kid, I had little exposure to hunting, which I imagined as a pastime for drunk slobs who wanted to massacre wildlife. When I grew up and became a parent myself, I was haunted by the specter of school shootings. The Columbine High School massacre in Colorado happened just two weeks after my first child was born in 1999; I held my tiny infant against me as I took in the horror on the news.
Not long after that, I set down roots in Park Slope, Brooklyn, where the default position on guns was: They’re bad; let’s get rid of them. We wondered: What if we stopped making them? Can we hold gun manufacturers liable for gunshot deaths? What about a buy-back program like Australia did? I readily participated in these conversations, even though I was not as extreme as some of my friends, who said things like: “No guns. Ever.” I thought some people should have guns, but only highly trained, background-checked professionals. At the time, I didn’t know anyone who had a gun—and the prospect of owning one myself never crossed my mind.
But since moving from one of the most liberal places in the country to a farm in a red part of upstate New York, my views on firearms have shifted dramatically. In fact, I’m actually thinking about getting a handgun...

ChatGPT Codex Voice + browser + Sites: an expert’s AI workflow | Nick Baumann (OpenAI)
Listen now on YouTube [ https://substack.com/redirect/02c141e4-574b-4443-b133-3c61315d7426?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] • Spotify [ https://substack.com/redirect/79213b21-3ea9-4ee4-9cff-6b14b940debf?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] • Apple Podcasts [ https://substack.com/redirect/b35bb6a8-e701-430a-afa7-2c22ed4c747d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Brought to you by:
Bolt.new [ https://substack.com/redirect/dc208b60-3193-465b-88c4-f1ee702f2079?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]—Turn your idea into a real product
Hyperagent [ https://substack.com/redirect/7e3c34ac-07b8-4a59-a2ed-d894544efa5d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]—Deploy fleets of agents that handle real work
Nick Baumann from OpenAI joins Claire to demonstrate how he uses ChatGPT, Codex, and Voice to automate huge parts of his work and life. He walks through advanced workflows for managing tasks in parallel, monitoring email and expenses, booking travel, building and publishing websites, and even turning dozens of raw clips into finished videos.
Biggest takeaways:
ChatGPT Codex Voice doesn’t just answer questions. It can actually operate your computer while you keep talking. Nick Baumann demos the new interface live: he triggers it with a hotkey, the orb reads what’s on his screen through Appshots, and Codex spins up separate threads to book a flight, file an expense report, and check his calendar at the same time. 
One of Codex’s most powerful features is also one of its least understood: thread-forking. When a task gets complicated, Codex can open a new thread, branch from an existing one, or pull context from previous conversations on its own. Users don’t have to manually organize everything first.
Heartbeats in ChatGPT Work offer a practical glimpse of always-on agents. Nick gets notified when a suspicious charge appears, a package is nearby, or an email needs his attention—and he set it all up without writing code.
ChatGPT Sites looks much closer to a real deployment platform than a lightweight demo. It includes a SQL database, file storage, environment variables, and email-based access controls. During the episode, Claire and Nick build and publish a live How I AI tips site, organized by tool and job function, in roughly the time it would normally take to set up a CMS template. For internal tools, small apps, and private resources, that starts to feel genuinely useful.
Nick’s video-editing workflow is one of the clearest examples of AI cutting real production work. He records 50 or 60 raw clips, uploads them, talks through the rough story he wants, and lets a custom plugin transcribe everything, scan the footage, choose the strongest takes, and assemble finished vertical videos overnight. What would normally eat up most of a content team’s day is largely handled while he sleeps.
Voice may be the best way to give AI context because it removes the pressure of figuring out exactly what to type. Claire calls this the “yapper’s API,” and the idea is simple: people often get more useful results when they talk freely than when they stare at an empty prompt box trying to be precise. Across two-person voice chat, mobile dictation, and Codex’s orb interface, the same pattern keeps showing up—people who talk to AI tend to give it more context, and more context usually leads to better work.
As AI gets more capable, latency is becoming a much bigger product decision. Nick often uses the highest-intelligence mode in Voice, but once a model has the tools it needs, speed can matter more than another small jump in reasoning quality. A lot of AI products are still designed around the assumption that waiting is unavoidable. As that changes, the tools that feel immediate will have a major advantage—especially for users who currently find AI too slow to bring into a live workflow.

Hi all,
Here’s our Monday roundup of data signals across AI, energy and markets.
Enjoy!
Know someone who should read Exponential View? Invite them to join.
Job boundaries are blurring. Nearly half of job-specific ChatGPT [ https://substack.com/redirect/ea4dbb97-7d6d-43f8-bf99-df6edf92748b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] tasks fall outside users’ primary occupation. 
Productivity follows use. Employees who use AI across several different use cases are twice as likely to report a positive impact on productivity [ https://substack.com/redirect/d5ae7e2c-4429-4ba2-838e-e0a760735101?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] than employees who use it for one or two types of tasks.
Agentic patents. Globally, patents for agentic AI use have grown 59% [ https://substack.com/redirect/b9958f5a-7f17-48d5-b01c-dabb332e126d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] in the last year – now making up 9% of AI application patents.
Value chain growth. While the S&P 500 companies are beating expectations by 27% this Q2, Bloomberg’s AI Value Chain companies come out at 71% [ https://substack.com/redirect/2f088cf4-5f1d-408d-b642-dfbd79d8e50d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Companies along the supply chain are outperforming incumbents.
Skilled shortage. The data center build-out in the US is facing a skilled-trades gap of 288,000 workers to meet demand [ https://substack.com/redirect/24645f4d-f198-4180-859c-9aa6acbd686a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] in 2027 if traditional construction methods continue. Higher premiums for these workers are increasing average earnings.
Entertained by AI. Over 95% of short dramas released in China in Q1 this year used AI in their production [ https://substack.com/redirect/7a60f8d3-11e3-4c17-bee6-d2d381a63cf3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Some users are starting to earn money by licensing their facial likeness in video content.
Temperature rises incoming. With the coming El Niño, climate scientists expect 2026 and 2027 to see record-high temperatures [ https://substack.com/redirect/a2cdd764-6cd8-4d63-b222-1828cb3598d3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
Economic effects are real. El Niños have historically intensified social unrest via food and energy supply shocks – unrest periods are closely correlated with food price spikes of 40-60% YoY [ https://substack.com/redirect/85ca9273-d237-4743-8d92-80eea12e0993?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
The yen threat. Japan spent an estimated $59 billion defending the yen last Thursday [ https://substack.com/redirect/ff3971df-d28c-4798-bcfd-f34432e5f71e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], with Washington expected to add $5 to $10 billion [ https://substack.com/redirect/4c7c2d78-84e4-448a-bdc7-dc7e7ffe6091?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] – the first joint yen purchase since 1998.
Socials beat study. The average 15-year-old in the OECD spends more time on social media [ https://substack.com/redirect/7ac8b97f-96db-4ee7-8dbc-2e2d8c5888a9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] than in lessons or homework combined.
Napoleon’s losses. A 422,000-man army marched to Russia in 1812, with only 10,000 making it back [ https://substack.com/redirect/a60d65ac-7310-4b89-bdba-62ed4ad4eabc?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] – this map shows the trajectory of the losses.

6 Culture Trends Worth Watching: Madonna, Avengers Doomsday, Million-Dollar
 Jackets, and More
1bc475994027ecf5.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.statsignificant.com/p/6-culture-trends-worth-watching-madonna

Welcome back to the Monday Roundup! 
The Monday Roundup is a weekly bonus edition featuring data-driven culture stories, curated datasets, and recommended reading. 
Your regular Wednesday essay stays free for everyone—this is strictly additive.
Today’s edition has six new data stories. Free readers get the first two; paid subscribers get the full thing, plus datasets and recommended reading. Enjoy!
In Today’s Roundup:
Original Data Stories: Madonna’s cultural renaissance, the entertainment industry’s ongoing wave of layoffs, the Emmys’ fading cultural relevance, the hype surrounding Avengers: Doomsday, country music’s Billboard takeover, and the million-dollar jacket.  
Recommended Reads: Notable data journalism and pop culture reads from around the web.
Unique Datasets: Ten publicly available datasets, covering everything from cataloged movie “jump scares” to Anthony Bourdain filming locations to Broadway attendance.
Trend 1: A Madonna Renaissance
Somehow, two things are true:
Madonna is back in the zeitgeist.
The year is 2026.
Over the past few weeks, Madonna has been the top artist trending on Reddit—and not for a tabloid scandal or a health scare, but for her music.
Among all legacy acts—that is, artists who released music before 1990—the queen of pop has seen the second-largest increase in monthly Spotify listenership in 2026.
The only singer to surpass Madonna in terms of newfound streaming interest is Michael Jackson, who is a) dead and b) the subject of an overwhelmingly sanitized biopic released this year.
Anyway, back to Madonna: how did a 67-year-old pop star find herself back in the cultural conversation? In short, she did the work.
Madonna has been on a press run for the ages in the lead-up to the release of her new dance album, Confessions II. The past few months have seen the ‘80s icon make a Coachella appearance with Sabrina Carpenter, perform at the World Cup halftime show, release a short film at the Tribeca Film Festival, stage an elaborate brand partnership with dating app Grindr, and mount several dance club pop-up performances.
The result has been a steady drumbeat of cultural interest, culminating in Confessions II debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard album chart.
If there ever were a playbook for a cultural figure to reclaim their place in the zeitgeist—without releasing a derivative biopic—then Madonna may have executed on this roadmap to perfection.
Trend 2: Entertainment Industry Layoffs
There is no business like show business. Every year, tens of thousands of industry hopefuls—be they actors, aspiring executives, or prop department enthusiasts—descend upon Los Angeles with the hope of “making it.” And while Hollywood has always been a crapshoot, the degree to which the industry is a crapshoot can vary by the week. During the streaming boom, Hollywood saw a period of sustained expansion unlike any other time in its history. And then the streaming bubble burst.
In early 2022, Netflix reported its first subscriber decline in more than a decade, sending its stock price tumbling over 50%. That disastrous earnings call, coupled with mounting concerns about inflation, convinced Wall Street that streaming’s era of boundless growth was over.
Since then, the industry has seen a litany of job cuts, including a Disney layoff two weeks ago that slashed hundreds of positions.
According to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, LA entertainment employment peaked in 2023, before myriad layoffs and strikes sent this figure to a 30-year low.
And I’m sure you’re looking at this and thinking to yourself, “How can this get any worse?” Well, the answer is that it most certainly can (and will), assuming Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. eventually goes through. Most likely, the numerous “synergies” between the two historic studios will yield more job loss when Warner-Mount inevitably needs to cut costs to pay back the oil magnates who financed the takeover.
I have no pithy joke to close this section; this simply stinks.
Trend 3: Do the Emmys Matter?
Open almost any streaming app, and you’ll be greeted by a glossy tile promoting that platform’s 2026 Emmy nominees. Year after year, HBO, Netflix, and Apple prominently showcase the programs recognized by television’s most prestigious awards show. Which raises an obvious question: do the Emmys matter?
The boring answer is yes. As long as streaming services continue touting their Emmy pedigree across digital banners and real-world billboards, this 77-year-old institution can plausibly claim cultural relevance.
However, the degree to which the Emmys ever mattered, and how that significance has changed over time, is far more debatable...

77d9e01caafaff03.subject: Does going viral sell cinema tickets?
77d9e01caafaff03.body:
View this post on the web at https://stephenfollows.com/p/does-going-viral-sell-cinema-tickets

A couple of years ago, Sony re-released a movie that had flopped only a few months earlier. 
Morbius  [ https://substack.com/redirect/9334281d-4656-43e4-83e2-6d27e7343ad9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]had died at the box office in April 2022, opening to $39.1m [ https://substack.com/redirect/bb5156d1-620a-481a-afd2-25e9c7977e6f?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and then dropping 74% in its second weekend [ https://substack.com/redirect/7cb6abe0-1f18-4dc4-8b46-7e796bda793a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. But over the following weeks, a meme playing on the film’s dreadful dialogue (’It’s Morbin’ time’ [ https://substack.com/redirect/de5ac282-5b3d-4a5d-89fb-d3f89ae318a9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]) had taken off. 
Sony read this massive increase in engagement as demand for the movie and decided to re-release it theatrically on 3 June. It did not do well.  The re-release took roughly $300,000 [ https://substack.com/redirect/3717a283-5770-4d5a-970a-b940fd35c049?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] across 1,037 cinemas, which works out as a per-screen average of $300, or 30 tickets over three days. Yikes.
And this is  not an isolated experience.  A number of movies have thrived and failed to capitalise on internet meme fame.  And yet, some of the biggest moments for cinema in the past few years have been driven by memes and outsized online interest.
So how can we separate the memes that mean money from the fads that fuel failure?
I have isolated 24 movie meme moments, from Barbie  [ https://substack.com/redirect/11f5a278-c6a6-4e89-a1d1-2c8576944390?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]to Cats [ https://substack.com/redirect/ddb1ec29-ffd6-49e2-a373-b72f87ad21a1?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], and looked for patterns in the wins and losses. After all that, there are some pretty clear lessons for studios and movie marketers.
I’m going to go through examples of both virality working and failing, talk about how studios try to manufacture these moments, and end with tips for how to know when a meme means money. 
Viral moments which did not drive Box Office
Let's start with an example in which a film's inclusion in a popular meme did not translate into box-office sales.
Cats (2019) is one of the biggest examples. When the first proper trailer dropped, the movie’s ‘digital fur technology’ sparked no end of online conversation and became a global punchline weeks before release. Then the film opened to $6.5m [ https://substack.com/redirect/c1ed0b62-2357-431b-8756-2b172ddabba9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] against tracking that had once hoped for $14m to $17m [ https://substack.com/redirect/dcaa4f14-fb7f-4c53-aeb9-cb7058de2335?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. 
The internet’s reaction to Cats’ fur somewhat mirrored the film press corps’ reaction to the full version of Megalopolis  [ https://substack.com/redirect/c0645973-82d9-4cec-a3f3-d3a290bfc098?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ](2024). Francis Ford Coppola’s self-financed opus cost $120m to make but opened to just $4m [ https://substack.com/redirect/886628bd-1c2b-40f0-b44b-5cb3d1db42cf?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] domestically. 
When PostTrak asked buyers [ https://substack.com/redirect/886628bd-1c2b-40f0-b44b-5cb3d1db42cf?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] why they had chosen to see the movie, 61% said ‘because of Coppola’, and only 9% said they had ‘heard it was good’. Megalopolis sold on morbid curiosity to a tiny audience of people who wanted to witness the car crash in person.
Snow White  [ https://substack.com/redirect/b4b0772a-eeb3-4aeb-8ccf-341c3c93ea36?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ](2025) probably had the longest and loudest run of pre-release bad headlines than any movie in recent history. So on the one hand, there was high awareness and a strong viral conversation, but on the other it was almost entirely negative. It opened to $42.2m [ https://substack.com/redirect/368f58ae-6280-4132-b07a-3f65def4a3b0?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] on a reported $336m budget and fell 66% in weekend two [ https://substack.com/redirect/719055aa-da5e-4b56-aab1-0286b8902cdd?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Being talked about constantly is not the same as being wanted.
These three examples all have one thing in common - the joke was that the movie was bad. But that’s not the main common thread in the memes which don’t convert to tickets.
Saltburn  [ https://substack.com/redirect/5f499ba3-7521-459b-96c3-4e85d5aa4230?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ](2023), because it went viral in a big way, with Saltburn-themed videos racking up nearly 4 billion views on TikTok [ https://substack.com/redirect/aa0fb7a3-43a7-44cf-9b2a-be8c2917b9f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], and Sophie Ellis-Bextor’s ‘Murder on the Dancefloor’ shooting back up the charts. Despite this, the film’s global Box Office takings were the same as its reported budget ($21.1 million vs $20 million).
The memes that could
Now let's look at some viral moments that did seem to drive success on the big screen.
Minions: The Rise of Gru [ https://substack.com/redirect/8f235dca-0ee1-4a45-88c1-4883f024861a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (2022) is the model. The ‘#GentleMinions’ [ https://substack.com/redirect/e423e65c-0ded-46e7-9cb3-0ffc9c73c806?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] trend had teenagers turning up to screenings in suits, filming themselves treating a kids’ cartoon like a black-tie event.
Illumination was expecting their movie to take $70m to $80m [ https://substack.com/redirect/deb30676-b356-4571-ba23-1177fb385857?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] over the four-day opening. It ended up taking over $125m [ https://substack.com/redirect/1b4e8e4b-55dc-45ef-86d2-9122c25b9a72?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. A key part of those extra audience members was, unusually for a Minions movie, 13-to-17-year-olds, who accounted for 34% of the opening audience [ https://substack.com/redirect/6242f776-7ec6-4a4e-9c1b-e840a6b9fa38?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], compared with just 8% for the previous film in the series.
A Minecraft Movie [ https://substack.com/redirect/0df74b44-a722-46c4-acd1-c76e44e4e660?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (2025) also tracked at $70m to $80m [ https://substack.com/redirect/4c167e98-7718-4edc-8c94-8f43457cb4bb?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] but opened even bigger than  The Rise of Gru, at $163m [ https://substack.com/redirect/0df74b44-a722-46c4-acd1-c76e44e4e660?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. The ‘chicken jockey’  [ https://substack.com/redirect/1ffac198-4863-4619-879e-88a723562a8d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]meme, in which audiences shout and throw popcorn at a specific line, erupted soon after its release, extending the film’s life on the big screen. Warner Bros leaned in, formalising it with official rowdy ‘Block Party’ screenings [ https://substack.com/redirect/095c5fb8-d1f4-4577-8301-e787379757b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] that gave people a fresh reason to go back.

726f6850ea115527.subject: Nike vs. Starbucks Turnaround: Two Ways to Break a Great Company
726f6850ea115527.body:
View this post on the web at https://gadallon.substack.com/p/nike-vs-starbucks-turnaround-two

Nike closed its fiscal year with $46.4 billion in revenue, flat against the prior year and down 2 percent.
Seven weeks earlier, Starbucks had reported net revenue up 9 percent to $9.5 billion and global comparable sales up 6.2 percent, its first quarter of growth on both the top and bottom line in more than two years.
Two iconic brands with two chief executives who started a month of each other in the fall of 2024.
Two turnarounds the market has filed under the same heading: great company stumbles, new leader arrives, great company recovers.
The conventional narrative is that both companies lost their way, hired the right person, and are now executing a comeback, and don’t get me wrong: there is truth in that. But at a closer look, they are quite different: Nike broke its strategy while Starbucks broke its operations. And they deserve a different treatment.
Here is my prediction: Within a few quarters, Starbucks will look healed while Nike still looks broken, and most commentary will read that gap as a verdict on the two management teams.
Two Ways to Break a Great Company
In 1980, Charles Hofer split business turnarounds into two kinds [ https://substack.com/redirect/3d08524f-c553-48e7-9033-7d6a02fe5ba2?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
An operating turnaround is about doing things right: cost, throughput, asset utilization, revenue per unit, and the machinery of execution all while keeping the strategy pretty much as before.
On the other hand, a strategic turnaround is about doing the right things: changing what the business actually is, which markets it serves, which channels it uses, what it sells, and to whom.
I know the distinction may sound academic … until you try to fix a company with the wrong one, at which point it becomes the whole game.
I think it should be clear that Nike’s decline was strategic (and self-inflicted).
Under its CEO at the time, John Donahoe, who ran the company from 2020 to 2024, Nike bet the brand on going direct. It pulled back from wholesale accounts, walked away from shelf space at retailers it had supplied for decades, and reorganized itself internally around consumer segments, men’s, women’s, and kids, instead of around sport. It leaned on its classic franchises, the Air Force 1, the Dunk, the Air Jordan 1, and let the innovation pipeline that had always justified the premium run dry.
Each and every one of those moves optimized something.
Direct sales carry a higher gross margin than wholesale. A leaner set of proven franchises is cheaper to produce than a constant stream of new silhouettes. The problem is that they optimized the wrong thing. While Nike was busy owning its customers, Hoka and On built running businesses out of nothing, New Balance turned into a lifestyle brand, and Adidas sold every Samba it could make. Nike vacated the field.
That is a strategy failure, and fixing it means changing what the company does.
Starbucks broke differently. Nothing was wrong with the idea of a coffee chain selling (bad) coffee at a premium in a comfortable room.  Instead, what decayed was execution.
Over several years, the mobile app and mobile ordering grew to a very large share of transactions, and in doing so, decoupled the moment a customer ordered from the moment they showed up.
That is a great feature for the customer ordering on the mobile, but a throughput nightmare for the store, orders arrive in bursts with no relationship to who is standing at the counter.  It’s also a nightmare to the occasional customer ordering in person. I remember ordering coffee at the Starbucks at Boston Logan Airport after the Boston Marathon, and getting a quote of 15 minute waiting time to get my coffee, when I was the only person standing in line.
Layer on a menu that had metastasized into tens of thousands of possible customizations, and a barista at peak is effectively running three or four fulfillment channels at once: the café line, the mobile queue, the drive-thru, and delivery. Wait times stretched.
The room that was supposed to be the product (aka as “The Third Place”), filled up with people staring at their phones, waiting for a name to be called.
The good news is that both declines were caused from the inside.
The turnaround research is fairly consistent that internally caused declines are more recoverable than externally caused ones, for the obvious reason that the firm controls the levers. Neither company was killed by its environment. Coffee did not go out of style, and the sneaker category did not shrink.
Each company did this to itself, which means each company can undo it. What differs is what “undo” requires.
One caveat belongs on the table before the diagnosis hardens, because internal causation is a matter of degree, not a switch: Nike’s overarching failure is endogenous, a strategy it chose.
It’s the worst single market, not.  In other words, Nike is running its recovery into a deeply problematic market in China: a soft consumer economy, and a nationalism that increasingly steers shoppers toward Anta and Li-Ning over Western brands.
Just to be clear: It does not change the diagnosis, only the degree of difficulty and the length of the clock.
The Retrenchment Both Are Refusing
Once you know which kind of turnaround you are in, the literature has a clear playbook for each one, but the front page is quite similar: retrench.
Robbins and Pearce, in their canonical 1992 study [ https://substack.com/redirect/05abc6bd-cd06-4694-9acb-c4aada2c4244?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], described turnarounds as a two-stage process. First retrenchment, the decline-stemming work of cutting costs and shedding assets to stop the bleeding. Then comes recovery, the growth-oriented work that follows. Pearce and Robbins later put it bluntly: retrenchment is the foundation [ https://substack.com/redirect/13674d83-4174-4535-ae32-9f3533856a2b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
Cut first, grow later.
But as usual in the academic literature, no orthodoxy go unchallenged.
Barker and Mone argued in 1994 that retrenchment is frequently a consequence of decline rather than a cause of recovery [ https://substack.com/redirect/0d2562e2-f01a-4993-b070-b1aaebde469d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], and that what actually turns a firm around is strategic reorientation, not the cost-cutting that tends to accompany it.
Schmitt and Raisch eventually reframed the whole debate in 2013 as a duality [ https://substack.com/redirect/d655f378-4699-4d05-8455-332a3007a0f4?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]: retrenchment and recovery are not a sequence you march through; they are complementary activities best run at the same time.
In other words, stop the bleeding and rebuild the muscle concurrently.
The empirical work that followed has been unkind to cost-cutting as a theory of recovery. Barker and Duhaime, studying firms that actually recovered, tied recovery to strategic change rather than to the depth of retrenchment [ https://substack.com/redirect/d3bd57ac-1353-48e8-944d-f70c4bfdf219?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Sudarsanam and Lai, tracking distressed UK firms, found the ones that recovered leaned on growth and investment strategies while the ones that stayed stuck leaned on cost-cutting and asset sales [ https://substack.com/redirect/b4341580-94a3-4921-9818-63de0b760df9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. And in a resource-based study of declining firms, Morrow, Sirmon, Hitt, and Holcomb found that the actions that restored value were strategic asset and resource moves, not operating cuts [ https://substack.com/redirect/ce69c9ba-e23d-40c6-86c8-5c8129224aa1?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3

2df9ed841471e47b.subject: The Battle for Michigan—and the Democratic Party. Plus. . .
2df9ed841471e47b.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/p/battle-michigan-democratic-party

It’s Monday, August 3. This is The Front Page, your daily window into the world of The Free Press—and our take on the world at large. Today: Zineb Riboua on what really caused Spain’s migration crisis. Josh Code sits down with the literature professor fired for teaching literature. Michael Oren breaks down Donald Trump’s latest Gaza deal. And much more.
But first: the battle for Michigan—and the Democratic Party.
The Democratic Party’s civil war will see a major battle this week. The action will be in Michigan on Tuesday, when progressive populist Abdul El-Sayed will square off against Haley Stevens, a moderate congresswoman, in perhaps the most watched Senate primary of the cycle so far. El-Sayed is running as a fierce critic of Israel and the political establishment, not DSA-endorsed but certainly DSA-adjacent. Haley Stevens is a far more conventional candidate, and has the backing of Michigan big hitters, including Governor Gretchen Whitmer.
The stakes are as high as the dividing lines are clear. The Democrats need to win the seat to stand a chance of taking control of the Senate. Victory for El-Sayed in a big, purple state like Michigan sets up the biggest test yet for the insurgent faction seeking to grab the reins of the Democratic Party.
Ahead of Election Day, we sent Olivia Reingold to Michigan to take the temperature of the race. Here’s what she found.
Matthew Yglesias watches Democratic Party infighting more closely than almost anyone. He’s a Democrat who says he’s tired of watching his party play what he calls “loser politics.” On the latest episode of Conversations with Coleman, he talks to Coleman Hughes about the state of the Democratic Party, the rise of democratic socialists, and much more. Don’t miss their conversation:
From a moderate Democrat to someone much further left: Eric Hovagim has worked with New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani and popular Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. Now he’s living in China, where he makes videos about why the United States is the “fourth Reich,” why Elon Musk is a “valid military target,” and what makes the Chinese Communist Party great. ###### OPENAI

#### 🤖 _**[OpenAI’s ‘Astra’ cracks long-open math problems](https://openai.com/index/ten-advances-in-mathematics/)**_

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/b4393f5d-0be6-46b5-a47e-72b939eb8ec0/ChatGPT_Image_Aug_3__2026__12_22_08_PM.png?t=1785739937)
Caption: Image source: Images 2.0 / The Rundown

**The Rundown: **OpenAI just [revealed](https://openai.com/index/ten-advances-in-mathematics/) that Astra, an internal version of its next major model family, solved 10 long-open math and computer science problems (one nearly 30 years old), covering geometry, group theory, quantum complexity, and more.

**The details: **

* Astra proved non-sofic groups exist, building the first symmetry structure that can’t be imitated by any finite shuffle, an exception hunted since 1999.

* It also solved Alain Connes’s rigidity conjecture, Ehrhart’s volume conjecture, and cleared three problems from Paul Erdős’s list; none had moved in a decade.

* Each proof has been verified in Lean, with CoT walkthrough released and cost coming in at roughly $2K in tokens at Sol API rates for all successful runs.

* In 24 hours, Anthropic’s Levent Alpoge [claimed](https://x.com/__alpoge__/status/2083855298239078748?s=20) he was able to reproduce five of the 10 proofs with Fable, running on a generic prompt and no internet.

**Why it matters: **The community is [debating](https://x.com/nicbstme/status/2083838614035689768?s=20) whether Astra’s proofs can be Fields Medal-worthy, given that a machine did the thinking here. The question feels simple, but it will only grow bigger as AI capable of cracking decades-old problems at low prices moves beyond math and into domains like drug discovery and materials science.

**The Rundown: **The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

**Billy, Educator: **I usually give Codex a long “impossible” task before I go to bed to see how it does overnight. This time, it finished it before I could even shut down my computer. I asked it to build a custom dashboard to monitor my 3D printer. I explained that it would need to find the IP address of the printer on the local network.

Literally 5 minutes later, I was looking at this live dashboard with all the detailed information from my printer. The future is wild.

**Brooke, Community Lead: **I just moved in with two friends. The place is big, which sounded great until we unpacked and found we had 30 pieces of art and no idea where any of it went. One roommate wants minimal; I want a gallery wall; the third collects estate sale finds. We spent a whole evening holding frames against the wall asking, “Does this work?” and got nowhere.

So I took pictures. Every room, then every piece laid out on the floor. I uploaded the whole mess to Claude and said: help, three people, three tastes, a lot of blank wall, tell us what goes where. It came back with groupings for all walls and actual reasons.
